sets.title: Turn It Down: Is Your Music Too Loud?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a magazine for young people:
partA.title: Turn It Down: Is Your Music Too Loud?
partA.text:
Earphones have become part of daily life for most teenagers. We wear them on the bus and even in bed. But medical experts are increasingly concerned that many young people are slowly damaging their hearing without knowing it.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), more than one billion young people around the world are at risk of hearing loss because they listen to loud sounds too often and for too long. The WHO says that listening at 85 decibels for eight hours, or at 100 decibels for just 15 minutes, can be harmful. Loud sound may first cause only a short ringing in the ears, but repeated exposure can make hearing loss permanent.

"The problem is that the damage happens quietly," explains Dr Helen Marsh, an audiologist who checks patients' hearing. "There is no pain, so at first you might only notice a ringing in your ears after a concert, or you keep asking friends to repeat themselves in a noisy restaurant."

So why do people turn the volume up? Some want to block out the noise of traffic or trains, while others say loud music helps them concentrate or feel more energetic. Sixteen-year-old Leo admits he often listens at full volume. "If I can still hear people talking around me, it isn't loud enough," he says.

Dr Marsh recommends a simple '60/60 rule': listen at no more than 60% of the maximum volume, for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

However, not all teenagers agree. "My grandparents can't hear well, and they never used earphones," says Leo. "I'll worry about it when I'm older."

sets.title: Fast Forward: Young Viewers Hit the Speed Button

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Fast Forward: Young Viewers Hit the Speed Button
partA.text:
When Form 5 student Chloe Tam sits down to watch a drama, she rarely watches it at normal speed. "I usually choose 1.5 times, sometimes double speed," she explains. "That way, I can finish a whole series in a weekend and still have time for homework."

Chloe is not alone. Most video apps now allow viewers to change the playback speed, and a survey of 600 local secondary students by the youth group Teen Screen Lab found that 58% often watch dramas or online videos faster than normal. Among these speed-watchers, the most common reasons were saving time (71%) and skipping 'boring' parts (45%). Students could give more than one reason.

Supporters say speed-watching is efficient and helps busy students keep up with popular shows, so they can join conversations with their friends. Some also use it when they revise with online lessons. "A recorded lesson that takes an hour only takes 40 minutes at 1.5 times," says one university student.

However, not everyone is a fan. A local film lecturer believes viewers miss a great deal. "Directors use silence, music and the expressions on actors' faces to tell a story. When you rush, you only follow the plot, not the emotions," he says. Some teachers also worry that students who speed through lessons may remember less, and that the habit is making young people less patient.

Chloe disagrees. "If a show is really good, I slow down and enjoy every scene. Speed is just a tool," she says.

So, is pressing the speed button a smart way to use our time, or are we losing something important?

sets.title: Strangers Next Door? Four Ways to Get to Know Your Neighbours

partA.sourceIntro: This list of tips appeared on a website for Hong Kong families:
partA.title: Strangers Next Door? Four Ways to Get to Know Your Neighbours
partA.text:
In a city where thousands of people can live in one building, many of us do not even know the names of the people next door. A recent survey by this website found that only one in four readers could name a neighbour on their floor. Yet good neighbours can help in an emergency, look after your flat when you are away, or simply make home feel friendlier. A smile and a 'good morning' in the lift is a good start, but here are four ideas that can bring the neighbours in a housing estate together.

1. Start a floor group chat
A group chat lets neighbours share news quickly, such as lift repairs or lost keys. Remember to set some rules so that it does not become too noisy, and help older residents who are not used to smartphones to join.

2. Set up a swap shelf
Put a small shelf in a shared area where people can leave books, toys or kitchen items they no longer need, and take something else in return. It saves money and reduces waste.

3. Organise a festival party
Mid-Autumn Festival and Lunar New Year are perfect times to invite neighbours to share snacks, make lanterns or decorate the building together.

4. Share your skills
Can you fix computers, cook a special dish or help children with homework? A weekly 'skill swap' lets neighbours teach each other something useful for free.

sets.title: Same Price, Less Inside: Shoppers Spot Shrinking Snacks

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Same Price, Less Inside: Shoppers Spot Shrinking Snacks
partA.text:
When university student Kelvin Ho opened his favourite bag of potato chips last week, something felt wrong. "The bag looked the same and the price was the same, but it seemed half empty," he said. He checked the label and found that the weight had dropped from 70 grams to 60 grams.

Kelvin had discovered "shrinkflation". This happens when a company makes a product smaller but keeps the price the same. Chocolate bars, toilet paper and cartons of juice have all been affected in different parts of the world.

A survey of 800 Hong Kong shoppers by the consumer group Smart Basket found that 64% believed some products they buy regularly had become smaller in the past two years. However, only one in four said they often check the weight on a package.

Companies say they have little choice. "The cost of ingredients, transport and rent keeps going up," explained a spokesperson for a snack company. "If we raised our prices, many customers would simply stop buying."

Not everyone accepts this. "Customers would rather see an honest price rise than be tricked," said Mandy Leung of Smart Basket. Some governments now require shops to warn customers. In France, for example, large supermarkets must put up a notice next to products that have become smaller but are sold at the same or a higher price.

Others say shoppers should simply be more careful. Comparing the "unit price", such as the price for every 100 grams, is one way to find the best value.

So, is shrinkflation a clever business decision or an unfair trick?

sets.title: Students Teaching Students: Why Peer Tutoring Works

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared on an education website:
partA.title: Students Teaching Students: Why Peer Tutoring Works
partA.text:
Ask any experienced teacher and they will probably tell you that the best way to learn something is to teach it to someone else. That is the idea behind peer tutoring, a system in which older students help younger ones with their schoolwork.

At one secondary school in Tsuen Wan, around 60 Form 5 students volunteer two lunchtimes a week to help Form 1 and Form 2 students with Mathematics and English. The scheme started three years ago with only eight tutors, but it has grown quickly because of positive feedback from both groups.

Form 2 student Jason Ip admits that he was nervous at first. "I didn't want to ask my teacher 'silly' questions in front of the whole class," he says. "With my tutor, I don't feel embarrassed, because she still remembers how difficult Form 1 was."

The tutors benefit as well. "When I explain a topic, I discover which parts I don't really understand myself," says Form 5 tutor Natalie Kwok. "I've also become more patient and more confident."

However, running a scheme like this is not always easy. Tutors have their own examinations to prepare for, and some lose interest after a few weeks. Teachers also need to check that tutors are explaining things correctly. A few parents worry that a schoolmate cannot take the place of a trained teacher.

To keep tutors motivated, the school gives them certificates and organises a thank-you lunch at the end of the year.

Could a similar scheme work at your school?

partA.sourceIntro: These survey results appeared in a school newsletter:
partA.title: Lunchtime Leftovers: What Our Survey Found
partA.text:
Every school day, many lunch boxes are returned to our lunch supplier with rice, vegetables and meat that nobody has eaten. To find out why, our Green Club surveyed 520 students from Form 1 to Form 6 about their lunch habits last month.

Almost half of the students (47%) said they leave at least a quarter of their lunch on most days. Junior form students left the most food. We then asked these students why, and they could choose more than one reason. The table shows their main answers.

Many students also shared ideas. "I'd eat everything if I could choose a smaller portion," wrote one Form 3 student. Another suggested a class competition to see who wastes the least. However, some students felt the problem was not their fault. "If the food tasted better, we wouldn't throw it away," said a Form 5 student.

At the moment, the supplier throws all the leftovers into general rubbish, so none of the food is recycled and it all ends up in landfills. This is a serious environmental problem: in Hong Kong, food waste is the largest type of everyday rubbish buried in landfills, making up nearly 30% of the total. Our lunch supplier says it can offer different portion sizes and a more flexible menu, but only if the school asks for this. The Green Club will send its ideas to the principal next month.

partA.sourceIntro: This page appeared on a website for young people in Hong Kong:
partA.title: Strike a Pose! Inside the Self-Photo Studio Craze
partA.text:
What is a self-photo studio?
Korean-style self-photo studios have become a hit with young people, and over the past few years many have opened in Hong Kong, in areas such as Mong Kok and Kwai Chung. There is no photographer. You and your friends go into a small room, choose a background, pick up a remote control and take your own photos. Most studios also have hats, glasses, wigs and other props that you can borrow for free.

Why do teens love them?
At one studio in Mong Kok, run by 24-year-old Kelly Ng, a basic session costs HK$128 for two people. "Most of our customers are secondary school students," says Kelly. "They come after exams, on birthdays or just because it's Friday. Some groups stay for over an hour trying on different props." Within minutes, you get a printed strip of four photos and a digital copy to share on social media. Many teens collect their strips in special albums or stick them on their phone cases.

What our readers say
"It's the best way to remember a day with friends. Photos on my phone just get lost in my gallery." – Mandy, 16

"It's fun, but I spent almost HK$500 last month. Some of my friends feel they have to go every weekend." – Jason, 17

"I prefer taking photos outdoors. It's free, and the views are real!" – Ivan, 15

Have you tried a self-photo studio yet? Tell us what you think in the comments below!

sets.title: Why I Pay My Kids to Do the Dishes

partA.sourceIntro: This blog post appeared on a parenting website in Hong Kong:
partA.title: Why I Pay My Kids to Do the Dishes
partA.text:
Last summer, after months of asking my two teenagers, Ethan (15) and Sophie (13), to help around the flat, I decided to try an experiment: I started paying them for their chores.

Here's how our new routine works. A price list is stuck on our fridge. Washing the dishes earns HK$10, cleaning the bathroom earns HK$30 and folding the family's laundry earns HK$15. Some jobs, such as making their own beds, remain unpaid, because I believe they are simply part of being a responsible member of the family.

The results have surprised me. Ethan now has a budget: he saves his chore money for new football boots and checks his savings every week. Sophie has discovered how much effort it actually takes to keep a bathroom clean, and she even reminds me to put my dirty clothes in the basket!

Not everyone supports my idea, though. My mother believes that children should help because they care about their family, not because they want to be paid. "What will happen when you stop paying them?" she asked. A colleague worries that money could change the relationship between parents and children, and that her own children would refuse to help without payment. And last month, Sophie asked whether she could pay her brother to do her chores for her!

Six months on, our home is tidier and the kids seem more grateful and understand the value of money better. But am I teaching them independence and hard work, or simply teaching them to expect a reward? I'd love to hear your opinions.

Grace Lau, mother of two

sets.title: Check! Can Chinese Chess Win Over Young Players?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online magazine for students:
partA.title: Check! Can Chinese Chess Win Over Young Players?
partA.text:
On a weekday afternoon in a small park in Sham Shui Po, a group of older men are crowded around a stone table, watching two players move their pieces and shouting advice at every turn. Scenes like this were once common across Hong Kong, but these days it is unusual to see a teenager joining in.

Chinese chess, also known as xiangqi, is a strategy game for two players. Each side controls 16 pieces, including horses, elephants and cannons, and a "river" runs across the middle of the board. The aim is to trap the other player's general. Although the basic rules can be learnt in an afternoon, experienced players say it takes years to play really well. It is taken seriously as a competition, too: xiangqi was even an official event at the 2010 Asian Games.

So why do so few young people play? "My classmates think it's a game for grandpas," explains Form 4 student Kenny Ho, who was taught by his grandfather. "Online games are faster and have much better graphics, so it's hard to compete with them."

However, there are signs that things are changing. Kenny's school chess club has grown from six to 25 members since it began organising lunchtime matches between students and teachers. A free app that introduces the basic moves through short puzzles has also become popular with beginners.

"It's like a battle in your head," says Kenny. "Once you win your first game, you'll be hooked."

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online entertainment magazine:
partA.title: Who Ruined the Ending? Teens and the Spoiler Problem
partA.text:
When a new local film opened in cinemas last month, Chloe, 16, had planned to watch it with friends that weekend. Two days before, however, a classmate posted a photo of the final scene in their class chat group. 'I still went, but the surprise was gone,' she says. 'It felt like someone had unwrapped my birthday present before I could.'

Her experience is far from unusual. In an online survey of 400 secondary students conducted by this magazine, 72% said a film, drama series or anime had been spoiled for them in the past year. Among these students, six in ten said it had happened in a group chat.

Not everyone is bothered, though. 'I often read the ending first,' admits Marcus, 17, 'because when I know what happens, I can relax and notice the small details.' Researchers are also divided: one study in the United States found that many readers enjoyed some short stories more when the ending was revealed in advance, while another found that spoiled stories felt less exciting.

Some apps now offer a solution. On certain chat platforms, users can hide part of a message as a 'spoiler', which others only see if they tap on it. Jason, 18, who manages an online group for anime fans, has also introduced a simple rule: nobody may discuss the ending until a week after a new episode is released.

Marcus, however, believes such rules go too far. 'If a film has been showing for a month, it's your responsibility to avoid the news, not mine to stay silent.'

partA.sourceIntro: These letters appeared in the readers' section of a local newspaper:
partA.title: Letters to the Editor
partA.text:
Don't leave older people behind

Dear Editor,

Last week my grandmother, who is 78, tried to make an appointment for a medical check-up, but the clinic told her she could only book through its mobile app. Although she owns a smartphone, the text is tiny, the buttons keep changing after every update, and she was terrified of pressing the wrong one. In the end she had to wait for me to help her, but I was at school all day.

More and more restaurants, banks and clinics now provide their services mainly online. For young people, this is quick and convenient. For many elderly people, however, it means feeling confused, embarrassed and shut out. Every organisation should keep a counter or a telephone line with a real person for those who need it.

Joyce Lam, Tsuen Wan

Going digital helps everyone

Dear Editor,

I understand Ms Lam's concerns, but going back to the old way is not the solution. I work as a receptionist at a clinic. Since we introduced online booking, patients no longer queue outside for hours, and our phone lines are available for urgent calls.

Older people are perfectly capable of learning. My 70-year-old father now video-calls his friends every day. What they really need is patience and regular practice. Families should spend time teaching them, and community centres could offer more free classes with large-print instructions.

Technology is part of everyday life now. Let's help everyone join in instead of slowing everyone down.

Raymond Ho, Sha Tin

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared on a website for Hong Kong parents:
partA.title: Same Slide, Same Swing: Are Our Playgrounds Too Boring?
partA.text:
Walk into many older housing estates in Hong Kong and you will probably discover the same playground: a short plastic slide, two swings, a soft rubber floor and a sign listing everything children are not allowed to do. 'No ball games.' 'No cycling.'

These playgrounds are certainly safe, but many children find them dull and predictable. 'My son is eight, and he complains that the slide is for babies,' says Mrs Cheng, a mother in Ma On Shan. In a survey of 300 parents conducted by this website, 62% said their children became bored at their local playground within 15 minutes, and almost half admitted that they sometimes travel to another district to find a more exciting one.

Playground designers believe children need a certain amount of challenge. Climbing walls, rope nets, and areas with sand and water allow children to test their abilities, build confidence and independence, and learn to judge risks for themselves. 'A small fall teaches more than a hundred warnings,' one designer explains.

Not everyone agrees, though. Some parents worry about injuries and feel young children need close supervision, while elderly residents who use the same park for exercise or relaxation complain about the noise. A modern playground also needs to be suitable for children who use wheelchairs, who often find little equipment that is accessible to them in older playgrounds.

Good public space should belong to everyone in the community. So what would a playground that works for all ages actually look like?

sets.title: After School, More School: Is Your Child Over-Tutored?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared on a website for parents:
partA.title: After School, More School: Is Your Child Over-Tutored?
partA.text:
It is 9:30 on a Tuesday night. Fifteen-year-old Kelly has just got home from her third tutorial class of the week, and she still has a page of maths homework to finish. "I'm tired all the time," she says. "But all my friends go, so I'm scared to stop."

Kelly is not alone. In our online survey of 850 local secondary students, 63% said they went to at least one tutorial class every week. Among these students, one in four spent more than six hours a week in classes outside school.

Tutoring can help. Some students need extra support in a weak subject, and a good tutor can share useful exam skills. However, too much tutoring can cause problems:

Less sleep. Late classes push homework and bedtime later and later.

No time for hobbies. Sport, music and family time are often the first things to go.

Less independent learning. Some students wait for a tutor to explain everything instead of working things out for themselves.

High costs. Several parents told us that tutorial fees take up a large part of the family budget.

"Parents often add classes because they are worried, not because their child needs them," says one secondary school teacher. "Before you sign up for another course, ask: is this class really helping?"

What do you think? Share your experience in the comments below.

sets.title: Three Ways to Say Goodbye to Plastic Bottles at School

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online magazine for young people:
partA.title: Three Ways to Say Goodbye to Plastic Bottles at School
partA.text:
Walk past the rubbish bins at any school after lunch and you will probably see the same thing: plastic drink bottles, many of them only half empty. Since April 2024, restaurants in Hong Kong have not been allowed to give out plastic straws or plastic cutlery, but on many school campuses, disposable plastic bottles are still everywhere.

So what can schools do to reduce this waste? We asked students and teachers at three secondary schools about the ideas they have tried.

1. Water refill stations
One school in Sha Tin replaced its old water fountains with refill stations that provide cold, filtered water, so students can bring their own bottles and fill them up for free. "It's convenient, and students no longer need to queue at the tuck shop," says a teacher there. However, the machines were expensive to install, and they need regular cleaning and maintenance.

2. School-designed bottles
At a school in Tai Po, art students designed a reusable bottle, which is sold at the tuck shop for $30. "People are proud to carry something their classmates created," says Form 5 student Jason. Unfortunately, some students lose their bottles within a few weeks and go back to buying drinks.

3. A bottle-return machine
A school in Kowloon City has installed a machine that collects empty plastic bottles for recycling. Each bottle earns a student one point, and 20 points can be exchanged for a snack or a pen. Fewer bottles ended up in the bins during the first month, but some students now buy extra drinks to collect more points.

Which idea do you think would work best?

sets.title: Half an Hour Outside: Will a Daily Break Work?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Half an Hour Outside: Will a Daily Break Work?
partA.text:
A secondary school in Tsuen Wan wants its students to spend 30 minutes outdoors every school day. Under the plan, students would leave their classrooms after lunch and go to the playground or the basketball courts. They could play ball games, walk around or simply chat with friends.

The principal says the idea came from concerns about students' health. "Many of our students go from home to school and back again with very little time outside," she says. The Department of Health recommends that students spend at least two hours outdoors each day, as this may help to prevent or delay short-sightedness. The school also hopes that a break from desks and screens will help students stay alert and focused in afternoon lessons.

Last month, the school tried the plan with four Form 2 classes for two weeks. In a survey afterwards, 84 of the 140 students who took part said they felt more alert after the break. "I got to know students from other classes for the first time," says Form 2 student Chloe.

However, not everyone is excited. Thirty-one of the 140 students said they felt too hot and sweaty to concentrate afterwards. To make time for the break, lunch would be 15 minutes shorter and school would finish 15 minutes later. "My son has music lessons straight after school, so this would change our whole family routine," says one parent. Teachers are also worried about how to supervise about 900 students on rainy days, when everyone would have to share one small covered playground.

The school will make a final decision after collecting more views.

sets.title: The Gift Swap That Went Wrong

partA.sourceIntro: This blog post appeared on a website for secondary school students:
partA.title: The Gift Swap That Went Wrong
partA.text:
Every December, my class holds a gift swap at our Christmas party. Everyone pulls a classmate's name out of a box and buys that person a present. It sounds harmless, doesn't it? Last year, it turned into a small disaster.

Because there was no budget, the presents were completely different in value. One lucky boy received wireless earphones worth about HK$700, while the girl whose name I drew got a HK$15 keyring from me. I saw the disappointment on her face and felt embarrassed, but it was honestly all I could afford that week.

Gift-giving had turned into a contest. Several classmates spent whole afternoons in shopping malls searching for something "good enough", and a few even borrowed money from their parents. By the end of the party, the bin was overflowing with wrapping paper, and at least six unwanted gifts were left behind on desks.

This year, our class teacher has asked us to design a fairer system. Here are some suggestions so far:
- a maximum price of HK$80
- a wish list of three ideas from every student
- handmade or second-hand gifts only
- as well as the swap, an old toy or book from everyone for a charity

Not everyone is convinced. My friend Derek believes a budget takes the fun out of the swap. "With only HK$80, everyone will buy the same boring snacks and stationery," he argues. Maybe he has a point, but a gift should be a kind act, not a race to spend more. I would rather have a fair swap than an expensive one.

sets.title: Sharing the Ride: Good Habits on Buses and Trains

partA.sourceIntro: This list of tips appeared in an online magazine for teenagers:
partA.title: Sharing the Ride: Good Habits on Buses and Trains
partA.text:
Every morning, thousands of students squeeze onto Hong Kong's buses and trains. We asked 380 readers which habit annoyed them most: 41% chose loud phone calls and 27% chose people blocking the doors. Here are our tips.

1. Let people off first
Stand beside the doors and wait for passengers to get off before you get on.

2. Take off your backpack
On a packed train, a big school bag can hit the people behind you. Hold it or put it down by your feet.

3. Keep your voice down
Use earphones for music and videos, and keep phone calls short. As one reader put it, "Nobody needs to hear about your dinner plans."

4. Think about the priority seats
These seats are for people in need, such as older people, pregnant women, people with disabilities and passengers with babies. Even in an ordinary seat, offer it to someone who needs it more. Not everyone agrees, though. "After eight lessons and football practice, I'm exhausted too," says Owen, a Form 5 student. "Why should students always stand?"

5. Save your snacks for later
Eating and drinking are not allowed inside the paid areas of MTR stations, and that includes the trains. Nobody enjoys the smell of curry fish balls in a crowded carriage.

6. Stand right, walk left?
Many people in Hong Kong stand on the right of escalators so that people in a hurry can walk on the left. However, for safety reasons, the MTR asks passengers to hold the handrail, stand on both sides and not walk at all. "But then I'll miss my train!" one reader complained.

sets.title: Is Anyone Listening? A School Radio Show Fights for Its Audience

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online magazine for secondary school students:
partA.title: Is Anyone Listening? A School Radio Show Fights for Its Audience
partA.text:
At 1:05 p.m. every school day, the speakers in the canteen of a secondary school in Sha Tin come to life with the words "Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to today's lunchtime show!" A pop song starts, and the student-run radio programme begins.

The problem is that fewer and fewer students are listening. When the school's radio club surveyed 260 students last term, only 15% said they listened on most days, and about four in ten said they could not hear the show clearly over the noise in the canteen. "Most of us just put our earphones in and watch videos on our phones," admitted Hugo, an S3 student.

The club's chairperson, Joanne Lui (S5), believes the content is the real issue. "For years we've done exactly the same thing: three songs, a few school announcements and the weather. Students can get all of that on their phones," she explained.

Now the club is planning a complete makeover of the programme. Ideas include a song request box, a weekly quiz with small prizes, birthday messages for classmates, and interviews in which teachers talk about their school days. Some members would also like students to host short shows themselves.

Not everyone is enthusiastic about the changes. A few teachers worry that live shows could go wrong, while some students say they would prefer a quiet lunch. "If it's too loud or silly, people will complain," warned one S6 student.

Joanne, however, remains optimistic. "Radio is about people and their stories, not just music," she said. "If students hear their friends on air, they'll start listening again."

sets.title: Low Battery? What to Know Before You Rent a Power Bank

partA.sourceIntro: This page appeared on a consumer advice website:
partA.title: Low Battery? What to Know Before You Rent a Power Bank
partA.text:
Rental power bank machines can now be found in convenience stores, shopping centres, restaurants and even some universities across Hong Kong. One large service alone has more than 5,000 stations in the city.

How does it work?
1. Scan the QR code on the machine with an app.
2. Pay a deposit or link a credit card, and a power bank pops out.
3. Charge your phone on the go, then return the power bank to any station of the same service.

What do users say?
"I'm out from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Once my phone died and I couldn't pay for anything or find my way. A rental power bank saved me." – Carmen, 17
"I don't want to carry a heavy power bank around every day." – Wing, 19
"Fifteen dollars here, twenty dollars there – it adds up. Buying my own would have been cheaper." – Toby, 16

Before you rent
• Check the price. Fees can be different from machine to machine, even for the same service, and some apps only show the price after you scan.
• Check the map. In a recent test, some apps showed the wrong location for return stations, which could mean wasted trips and paying for extra time.
• Check the battery. Make sure the power bank is charged before you walk away.

Our view: Renting is handy in an emergency, but if you rent every week, owning a power bank may make more sense.

partA.sourceIntro: This text appeared on the website of a local volunteer group:
partA.title: Neighbourhood Lifesavers: Be Ready to Help
partA.text:
Would You Know What to Do?

An old man falls down at a bus stop and does not get up. People stop and look, but nobody steps forward to help a stranger. Before an ambulance arrives, the first few minutes can make a big difference.

We are Neighbourhood Lifesavers, a team of volunteer nurses, students and former teachers in Sha Tin. Last year we asked 500 people in our area what they would do in a situation like this. Just 20% said they would feel confident giving first aid. Their main reasons for not helping were:
- "I'm afraid of doing something wrong and making it worse."
- "I don't know how to use an AED."
- "Someone else will probably help."
- "I'm worried about being blamed."

The good news is that you don't need to be a doctor. An AED is a machine that can give a shock to help a person's heart beat normally again, and it tells you what to do at every step. Every MTR station has them, and a government website shows where many others are.

Our free two-hour sessions teach you how to call 999, do chest presses to keep blood moving (CPR), use an AED and help someone with food stuck in their throat. You will not get a certificate, but most people leave feeling ready to act.

"I used to walk past and hope someone else would help," says Hailey, 16. "Now I'd know what to do first."

"Two hours isn't enough," one parent told us. "I'd be scared I'd forget everything."

Bring our campaign to your school: invite@example.hk

sets.title: Shirt or Tracksuit? Tai Po School Lets Students Choose

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Shirt or Tracksuit? Tai Po School Lets Students Choose
partA.text:
At the gate of a Tai Po secondary school each morning, you now see two kinds of students: some in white shirts and ties, others in blue tracksuits.

Since September, students have been free to choose daily between the formal uniform and their PE kit. Nobody has to wear PE kit, but the formal uniform is still required for school photos, speech day and visits outside school.

"After football at lunch, my shirt was always wet with sweat in class," said Form 2 student Jasper Choi. "In a tracksuit, I can play as hard as I like and still feel comfortable."

Not every student has made the switch. "When I'm wearing a shirt and tie, I feel focused, but in a tracksuit I feel as if I'm relaxing on the sofa at home," said Form 5 student Hazel Yip, who has worn her PE kit only twice.

Parents are divided as well. "Tracksuits just go in with the rest of the laundry, so there's no more ironing shirts late at night," said Mrs Tsoi, whose two sons study at the school.

One father, however, pointed out a hidden cost. "My daughter now wants three sets, because one set starts to smell after a hot, sticky day, and they aren't cheap."

Some former students are worried about the school's reputation. A man who graduated in 1998 was surprised when he noticed students on a bus last month.

"Our uniform used to tell everyone who we were," he explained. "In those tracksuits, I can't even recognise which school they come from."

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online magazine:
partA.title: Lights Out at Eleven? The Debate Over Hong Kong's Night Signs
partA.text:
Hong Kong's glowing signs appear on postcards and in films worldwide. But for people who live next to them, the lights can be a real problem.

"A huge video screen across the road shines into my bedroom until after midnight," says Wong Siu-ling, who lives in Mong Kok. "Even with thick curtains, I can't sleep properly."

Scientists call this light pollution: too much light from lamps, signs and screens at night. Bright lights can disturb residents' sleep, and they can also make birds that fly at night lose their way. Local university researchers have described Hong Kong as one of the world's most light-polluted cities.

Hong Kong already has a voluntary scheme for this, but it is not a law. Since 2016, thousands of shops, malls and offices have promised to switch off lights used for decoration and advertising from 11 p.m. or midnight until 7 a.m. Now some residents want a law that every business must follow, even shops that are still open.

Supporters say such a law would save electricity, help residents sleep and let city children see a few more stars.

Business owners, however, see things differently. "If our sign goes dark, people think we're closed," says Mr Lo, who runs a late-night noodle shop in Jordan. "My busiest time is after eleven."

Some people in the tourism industry also worry that visitors come to Hong Kong partly for its famous night views. And a few residents say that brightly lit streets make them feel safer walking home late.

So should the city become darker?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Running Together: Young People Find Friends on the Promenade
partA.text:
Every Thursday evening, about 50 people gather on the waterfront promenade in Tseung Kwan O for a free five-kilometre run. Most participants are in their teens or twenties, and many first came alone.

The group was started last spring by university student Ruby Kwan. "I wanted to improve my fitness, but running by myself was boring," she explained. "Now people come for the exercise and stay for the conversation." After each run, many members continue chatting over bubble tea at a nearby café.

Similar running groups have become popular with young people in many cities. Members say that a regular meeting time and a supportive crowd give them the motivation they lack on their own. "If I don't show up, someone messages me," said Form 6 student Brian Chiu, 17. "That's why running has finally become part of my weekly routine."

The organisers keep things simple and safe. Runners join a slow, medium or fast group according to their pace, so beginners are never left behind, and an experienced volunteer always jogs at the back of each group.

There are concerns, too. Some parents are uncomfortable with teenagers exercising in the evening alongside adults they hardly know. Some residents also complain that large groups block narrow paths shared with walkers. Brian's mother admits she was nervous at first. "Now that I know he's with a group and home by nine, I'm more relaxed," she said.

Ruby hopes more schools will form their own groups. "You don't need special talent," she said. "You just need a pair of running shoes and someone to run with."

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in an online magazine for young people:
partA.title: Subscribed and Forgotten: Are You Paying for Things You Don't Use?
partA.text:
Music, videos, cloud storage, mobile games, language apps – for many young people, life now runs on monthly subscriptions. But are they good value?

When a local youth consumer group asked 450 people aged 16 to 25 in Hong Kong about their spending, the average person had four subscriptions. More than 200 of them said they had at least one subscription they had not used in the past month. About one in three had to pay after forgetting to cancel a free trial.

"Each subscription looked cheap, so I never thought about it," said university student Yvonne Cheuk. "Then I checked my bank account and found I was paying almost three hundred dollars a month."

Supporters say subscriptions are often the better deal. A music app gives users millions of songs for a small monthly fee, students can get discounts, and family plans let several people share the cost. "I'd rather pay a little each month than buy expensive software I'll only use for one school project," said Form 5 student Jacky Ng.

Critics say companies make subscriptions easy to start but hard to stop. Some apps hide the cancel button deep in the settings, and prices can go up at renewal time. Over a year, the total can be surprisingly high, and users never actually own anything they have paid for.

The group suggests checking your bank account every month and setting a phone reminder a few days before a free trial ends.

partA.text:
Agnes Yuen, 68, retired cook
Every Lunar New Year, Agnes spends two whole days making turnip cake – which is actually made from white radish – for her big family. Her grandchildren help to wash the radishes and stir the mixture. "It's hard work, and my kitchen gets very hot," she says. "But it's the only time all of us cook together."

Wilson Fok, 17, Form 5 student
Wilson's family buys rice dumplings for the Dragon Boat Festival from a shop near their home. "Both my parents work long hours, and our kitchen is tiny," he says. "The shop ones taste good, and we only buy what we need, so nothing goes to waste."

Mabel Siu, 36, office worker
Last December, Mabel and her seven-year-old daughter joined a weekend workshop at a community centre to make sweet rice balls for the Winter Solstice Festival. It cost $150 each. "The teacher explained what the festival means, which I never really knew," she says. "It wasn't cheap, but my daughter still talks about it."

Dickson Lo, 24, graphic designer
Dickson taught himself to make snow-skin mooncakes by watching online videos. "My first ones fell apart, and I wasted a lot of ingredients," he laughs. "Now I make them with friends every Mid-Autumn Festival. We try new flavours like chocolate and mango, and give boxes to our neighbours."

partA.sourceIntro: These letters appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Escape Rooms: Two Readers Disagree
partA.text:
Not Just a Game

Dear Editor,

Last Saturday, my twelve-year-old daughter went to an escape room in Kowloon Bay for a friend's birthday party, and she came home in tears. The room was dark and the music was loud, and halfway through, a staff member dressed as a ghost jumped out of a cupboard. Nobody had warned us parents that the theme was a "haunted hospital".

I understand why these games are popular. Players work together to discover clues and solve puzzles before time runs out, often within 60 minutes. However, I have other concerns too. The room was on the ninth floor of an old industrial building with narrow stairs, and each ticket cost $230.

I hope escape room businesses will provide clear age advice and inform customers about frightening themes before they book.

Angela Fung, Tsing Yi

Give Escape Rooms a Chance

Dear Editor,

As a youth worker, I have taken more than ten groups of teenagers to escape rooms. For an entire hour, nobody looks at a phone, because they need to listen to each other, share ideas and stay calm while the clock is ticking. Last month, the quietest girl in one group solved the final puzzle.

Not every room is scary, since many have themes such as a detective's office, a space station or a toy shop at night. In the rooms I have visited, there was always an emergency button, and players could leave whenever they wanted.

Parents should ask questions before booking, but they should not treat escape rooms as dangerous.

Cyrus Shum, Tai Wai

sets.title: Hot Day? How to Keep Your Cool

partA.sourceIntro: These tips appeared on a health website for teenagers:
partA.title: Hot Day? How to Keep Your Cool
partA.text:
Hong Kong summers are long, hot and humid, but school life does not stop for the weather. PE lessons, sports practice and outdoor trips often carry on even when the Hong Kong Observatory has issued the Very Hot Weather Warning. When a sports charity surveyed 320 secondary students about hot days at school, 43% said they rarely drank water during PE lessons, and about two in three said they had felt dizzy or very tired after outdoor activities.

1. Sip water all day
Carry a water bottle and take small sips throughout the day. Do not wait until you feel thirsty.

2. Dress light
Loose, light-coloured clothes help your body lose heat. Outdoors, a wide-brimmed hat or an umbrella gives you shade.

3. Protect your skin
Use sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30, and put more on after sweating.

4. Plan around the sun
If you can, do outdoor activities in the morning or late afternoon, not at midday.

5. Take breaks in the shade
Rest in a cool place during long games or practice. A short break is not a sign of weakness.

6. Know the warning signs
A headache, dizziness or feeling sick can mean your body is getting too hot. Stop, move to a cool place and tell a teacher straight away. Heatstroke is a medical emergency.

Some students say a big bottle makes their school bag too heavy, or that they do not want to stop in front of their teammates. Looking out for each other can make a real difference.

sets.title: Fridays Off: Design Firm Tests a Four-Day Week

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Fridays Off: Design Firm Tests a Four-Day Week
partA.text:
A small design company in San Po Kong has given its 18 employees an extra day off every week without reducing their salaries.

Since March, its staff have worked from Monday to Thursday only. According to the founder, the six-month experiment began after two of her most talented designers resigned to take less stressful jobs. "Everyone was exhausted and making careless mistakes," she explained. "We wanted to find out whether we could work more efficiently and finish the same amount of work in four days."

The results look positive. The company reports that employees are more focused, take fewer sick days, and most projects are delivered on time, partly because meetings have been shortened from an hour to 30 minutes and staff check emails only three times a day.

Designer Phoebe Chong, 27, spends her Fridays visiting her grandmother and attending a dance class. "I return on Monday full of creative ideas," she said.

The change has brought problems too. Some staff now work ten-hour days to finish their tasks, and several clients have complained that it is inconvenient when nobody answers the phone on Fridays. "If something urgent happens on a Friday, I have to wait until Monday," said a restaurant owner who uses the company's services.

Trials of shorter working weeks have been held in countries such as the UK and Iceland. A local business lecturer pointed out that the idea may suit office jobs but would be far more difficult for hospitals, shops and public transport, which need staff every day.
